paragraphs: Fostering for children from Gloucester is arranged by Gloucestershire County Council, whose fostering recruitment team is based in the city at Shire Hall, and by the independent agencies shown above. The council says it most needs long-term homes for children over five, carers for brothers and sisters who need to stay together (which means more than one spare room), homes for children over ten and teenagers, regular short breaks for older children, and carers for children with disabilities or additional needs.

The council's route in has five steps. A first call may be answered by Fostering South West, a government-funded regional hub that the council runs with 14 other councils from the Isles of Scilly to Bournemouth, which then passes you to the Gloucester team. A home visit, application, checks and a medical follow, with an assessment that the council says usually takes about six months, alongside six Skills to Foster training sessions. A fostering panel then makes a recommendation and the head of the fostering service decides.

Once approved, council carers have a mentor from the start, extra support from a social worker and a family support worker in the first three months, then a supervising social worker, help available 24 hours a day, local support groups, a group for carers' own children and membership of The Fostering Network. The council also runs the Mockingbird programme, in which fostering families support each other around an experienced hub carer.

Gloucestershire's published payment information did not give a dated scale that we could check, so ask the council and two or three of the agencies above to explain their fees, training and local support before you choose.
